rawTranscript:
"Let me adjust my chair... alright. If you want to make Rose’s real Sunday Pot Roast, the kind that filled the whole house on Sunday afternoons, you have to remember the blizzard of 1968. We were snowed in for four days straight up in Buffalo, and your Uncle Frank had to shovel out the driveway three times just to get to the butcher shop! He brought back a massive, beautiful four-pound chuck roast. That’s what you need—a four-pound beef chuck roast. Don't let them give you a lean cut; you need that nice marbling or it turns into leather!
First thing you do, pat it dry and season it heavily. Now, Rose never touched a measuring spoon for this. She would pour coarse salt right into the palm of her hand—about a tablespoon—and rub it all over the meat along with a good tablespoon of cracked black pepper. Get a heavy cast-iron pot. Rose used her heavy orange Dutch oven that she inherited from her mother. Heat up two tablespoons of vegetable oil until it's shimmering, then sear that meat. Don't rush it! It needs about five minutes on each side until it forms a deep, dark brown crust. Uncle Frank always said the crust is where all the magic lives.
Once it's seared, pull the meat out and toss in the vegetables. You’ll need three large yellow onions, chopped rough, and about four big carrots cut into thick chunks. Don't dice them small or they'll vanish into the gravy! Stir them around in the beef fat until they get a little color. Then, grab two cloves of garlic—crush them with the flat side of your knife and drop them in.
Now, here is the secret step: Rose didn't use store-bought beef broth. She would take her favorite vintage porcelain coffee cup—the one with the faded blue flowers—and fill it with boiling water, then mix in two heavy tablespoons of tomato paste and a big glug of Worcestershire sauce. Let's call it two tablespoons. Pour that right into the pot to deglaze the bottom, scraping up all those beautiful browned bits with a wooden spoon. If it was a special occasion, Rose would sneak in a half cup of dry red wine, whatever Frank was drinking, to rich up the gravy. You can add that if you want it extra rich.
Put the beef back into the pot, nestling it right among the vegetables. Throw in two fresh sprigs of rosemary and a fistful of fresh thyme leaves. Cover it up tight. In 1968, our old oven door didn't seal right, so Rose would wrap a damp kitchen towel around the lid rim to keep the steam from escaping! But in your modern oven, just slide the covered pot in at 325 degrees. Leave it alone for three and a half hours.
You'll know it's ready when you can pull the meat apart with nothing but a dull dinner fork. We always served it over a mountain of buttery mashed potatoes while Uncle Frank complained about the heating bill and the Buffalo snow."

rawTranscript:
"Let me find my glasses... ah, here we are. Now, if you want to make Eleanor’s true Sunday Apple Crumb, you have to understand it didn't start in a kitchen; it started in Uncle Arthur's orchard back in the autumn of 1952. Arthur had just come home from the shipyard, and he brought us two massive crates of bruised McIntosh apples. He told us if we didn’t bake them by Tuesday, the pigs would get them!
So, your great-grandmother Eleanor sat right at the wooden table and peeled them all by hand. You’ll need six large apples—McIntosh if you want that classic mushy texture, but your Cousin Sarah always swears by mixing in two tart green ones to cut the sweet. Peel them, core them, and slice them into thick wedges. Don't make them thin, or they turn to absolute baby food in the oven!
Toss the slices right into a buttered baking dish. Eleanor always used that old chipped blue ceramic dish she got for her wedding. Now, listen closely because this is where people mess up: you dump in about a half cup of white granulated sugar, but then you need a heavy-handed pour of dark molasses. About two glugs—let's call it a quarter cup. If Arthur was in the kitchen, he’d try to sneak a splash of dark rum in there too, saying it kept the autumn chill out of the bones. You can add a tablespoon of rum if you want to honor him! Stir that up with a tablespoon of ground cinnamon and a tiny pinch of ground cloves. Just a pinch, mind you! Cloves are loud.
For the topping, Eleanor never used a measuring cup. She used her favorite chipped porcelain coffee mug. It holds about a cup and a half of all-purpose flour. Mix that in a bowl with one cup of rolled oats—the old-fashioned kind, not that instant dust. Then add a cup of packed dark brown sugar.
Now for the fat. In 1952, butter was treated like gold, so Eleanor used half unsalted butter and half lard. But today, just use a whole stick and a half of ice-cold unsalted butter—that’s twelve tablespoons. Cut it into tiny cubes and work it into the flour mixture with your bare fingers until it looks like coarse gravel. Your Aunt Clara always complained that her hands were too warm and melted the butter, so she used two butter knives to cut it in. If the crumbs don't clump when you squeeze them in your fist, throw in another cold knob of butter.
Spread that crumble thickly over the top of the apples. Bake it at 375 degrees. Our old wood-burning stove took hours, but in a modern oven, it takes exactly forty-five to fifty minutes. You'll know it’s done when the apple juices bubble up like molten lava around the edges and the top is a deep, golden mahogany brown. We used to serve it with heavy cream poured right out of the jar while we listened to Arthur tell stories about the ships down at the harbor."

title: Grandmother's Secret Apple Crumb Cake

ingredients.imperial: 4 medium apples, chopped into bite-sized chunks
ingredients.notes: Don't chop too small so you can bite into them
Tossed over apples while they sit
Melted thoroughly to overcome cold winter drafts
Mixed with melted butter till like wet sand

instructions.instruction: Preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
instructions.tip: Preheat early so the oven heats the chilly winter kitchen.

instructions.instruction: Chop 4 Granny Smith (or Honeycrisp) apples into hearty chunks—don't make them too small so you can bite into them.
Toss the chopped apples in a bowl with 1 cup of brown sugar and 1 solid tablespoon of ground cinnamon while they sit.
Completely melt 1 stick of unsalted butter in a small pan.
instructions.tip: Grandma's Trick: 'The apartment was so cold that the butter was hard as a rock, so we learned to melt it completely.'

instructions.instruction: Mix the melted butter into 1 cup of flour with a fork until it resembles coarse wet sand.
Transfer the spiced apples to a baking dish, scatter the crumb topping evenly over the fruit, and bake for 45 minutes, or until it smells like heaven. Serve piping hot while watching the snow fall.

nostalgia.summary: Your grandfather absolutely loved this back in the winter of 1974 when they lived in that drafty little apartment on 4th street.
anecdotes: The apartment on 4th street was so cold that butter was always hard as a rock, prompting the melted butter crumble technique.
They used to eat it hot straight out of the oven while watching the snow fall outside on 4th street.
nostalgia.secretFamilyTip: Melt the stick of butter completely before stirring into the flour so the crumble has that perfect wet sand texture.
